# 3.3: Periodic Truck Shipments

ISE 754: Logistics Engineering, Fall 2026

Carrying inventory costs money; transporting empty air is inefficient. Optimal shipment size is the best balance of the two.

No new Julia packages used.

New Logjam functions used

- aggshmt: Aggregate multiple shipments into a single equivalent shipment.
- minTLC: Independent shipment size that minimises total logistics cost (TLC), checking TL only, LTL only, or both modes depending on which arguments are provided.
- totlogcost: Calculate total logistics cost (transport + inventory).

## 1. Periodic shipments

Lecture 3.2 was about one-time shipments, where the shipper makes an operational decision: they know the shipment size $q$, and they know when and how much to ship. Periodic shipments call for a tactical decision instead: the shipper must determine the size $q$, and so will need to determine how often and how much to ship. The one-time decision can largely be left to a facility’s transportation department. Deciding how much to ship is more likely to fall to an industrial engineer, because it is a supply chain analysis rather than an execution task. Once the size is decided, someone else can choose among carriers, perhaps the one with the better contract.

The size is worth deciding because freight is lumpy, and the lumpiest part of it is the driver. Trucking depends on paying a driver for every trip, which is what makes big trucks and makes a big load much cheaper to ship than a small one. So every shipment carries a large fixed cost, and how much to ship is a trade-off between spreading that cost and not having enough on hand. Driverless trucks would let smaller loads move economically and shrink the problem, but for now it is a real decision. A household living next door to a grocery store treats the store as its pantry and plans nothing; one living twenty miles out and shopping once a week has to decide how much to buy, because each trip is a big fixed cost. Trucking is the same.

When demand for truck transport between origin-destination (O-D) points occurs repeatedly over a period of time, multiple demands are usually combined into shipments that occur periodically. Multiple demands are combined into single shipments because of the economies of scale associated with truck transport. Unlike a one-time shipment, where its size and time of occurrence is predetermined, periodic shipments require that the size and interval between shipments be determined. The exact timing and size of each shipment is determined by considering both the total transport costs (TC) and the total shipment-related inventory costs (IC), or what is termed the total logistics cost:

$$
TLC = TC + IC = n\,c + IC
\tag{1}
$$

where

- $n$ = $\dfrac{f}{q}$, average shipment frequency (1/yr)
- $t$ = $\dfrac{q}{f}$, average shipment interval (yr)
- $f$ = expected annual demand (ton/yr)
- $q$ = average shipment size (ton)
- $c$ = transport charge (\$).

From a tactical point of view, a one-time shipment is the exception. A manufacturer has regular suppliers and regular customers, so its freight moves on some frequency rather than as one-off shipments. When the manufacturer is the customer, receiving goods from a supplier, and it controls how those goods are shipped to it, it has a choice to make about how frequently to receive them: a truckload every day, every week, every two weeks, or once a month. The two sides of that choice pull in opposite directions. The supplier might want to send large truckloads, because they are more convenient for it to ship. From the customer’s point of view it would be much better to receive smaller quantities, because the cost of carrying the inventory that a large shipment brings is too high. Determining the best frequency for a shipment means finding the balance between the two, and since a frequency $n$ fixes the shipment size $q = f/n$, it is the same decision as choosing how much to ship each time.

Since there is no cost savings associated with using more than a single truckload for each periodic shipment, a truck’s maximum payload provides an upper bound on the size of each shipment:

$$
q \le q_{\max}
\tag{2}
$$

where

- $q_{\max}$ = maximum payload of a truck (ton), from Lecture 3.2.

As a result, the number of shipments per year equals the number of truckloads. Note that this number is not restricted to integer values, which is reasonable if the demand will continue indefinitely. The reason is that the unit of time should not affect the result. A year is only the unit chosen for convenience. Measured per month instead, the same demand is a fraction of a truck, and rounding it to a whole number of trucks each month gives a different annual total from rounding per year. Measured per week or per day it would round to zero, as though nothing ever needed to ship. So for a tactical decision the answer must be independent of the unit of time, and rounding in any unit breaks that.

Whether to round depends on the level of the decision. An operational decision is executed: orders are written and trucks go, so it is almost always discrete, since there is no fractional truck. Even there a fraction can be handled by breaking the load into pieces: a one-time shipment that fills, say, 3.27 truckloads can go as three full truckloads, with the remaining 0.27 of a load sent less-than-truckload (LTL). A fraction in a periodic shipment, such as the 3.27 truckloads a year of Ex. 1(a) below, is not that kind of fraction: it is only an artifact of choosing a year as the unit of time, and with a month or any other period it would not occur, so nothing is left over to ship. A tactical decision is planning for a future that is not known, so the number of trucks is never actually executed, and quantities such as demand keep their fractional values. At the strategic level the only things rounded are those that must physically be discrete: a firm cannot locate 3.2 facilities, however long the horizon. The one rule to take away is to keep the fractions.

Example 1: Periodic truck shipment from Raleigh to Gainesville

A product is shipped in cartons from Raleigh, NC (27606) to Gainesville, FL (32606). Each identical carton weighs 40 lb and occupies 9 ft3 (its cube). The linear dimensions of each unit are not known for truckload (TL) and LTL, and the cartons can be stacked on top of each other in a trailer. Additional information and data is presented only when it is needed to determine an answer.

Going from a one-time shipment to periodic ones needs some idea of demand, which, as in the location problems, is always the key input. It is also the input most often guesstimated: a detailed market survey and forecast is rare, and demand is the one thing everybody is fuzzy about. Here the example assumes a constant annual demand of 20 tons.

Example 1(a): Full truckloads per year

Continuing with the example, and assuming a constant annual demand for the product of 20 tons, determine the number of full truckloads per year, and account for why this number should not be rounded to an integer value.

```julia
# Code block 1: full truckloads per year
# From Example 1 of Lecture 3.2:
uwt = 40                           # lb
ucu = 9                            # ft^3
@show s = uwt/ucu                  # lb/ft^3
Kwt = 25                           # ton
Kcu = 2750                         # ft^3
@show qmax = maxpayld(s; Kwt = Kwt, Kcu = Kcu)  # ton

# New:
f = 20                             # ton/yr
q = qmax                           # ton (FTL => q = qmax)
@show n = f/q                      # TL/yr
```

```text
s = uwt / ucu = 4.444444444444445
qmax = maxpayld(s; Kwt = Kwt, Kcu = Kcu) = 6.111111111111112
n = f / q = 3.2727272727272725
```

```text
3.2727272727272725
```

$n$ is the average shipment frequency, and is not restricted to integer values.

$n =$ 3.2727 TL/yr, each a full truckload of $q = q_{\max} =$ 6.1111 ton.

Example 1(b): Shipment interval

Determine the shipment interval, and how many days there are between shipments.

The interval is the reciprocal of the frequency:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t &= \frac{1}{n} = \frac{q}{f} && \text{(yr/TL), average shipment interval} \\
t \times 365.25 &= \frac{365.25}{n} && \text{(day/TL), with 365.25 day/yr}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

The interval is one over the frequency, and the days between shipments are the interval in years times 365.25. The quarter day is there because the calculation is not tied to a particular year, which may or may not be a leap year: one year in four is, so using 365.25 keeps all of the accuracy.

```julia
# Code block 2: shipment interval
@show t = q/f                      # yr/TL
@show 365.25/n                     # day/TL, days between truckloads
```

```text
t = q / f = 0.3055555555555556
365.25 / n = 111.60416666666667
```

```text
111.60416666666667
```

$t =$ 0.3056 yr/TL, about 111.6 days between truckloads.

A baseline frequency of roughly three trips per year sounds operationally manageable, but service agreements often impose a minimum frequency, so the interval between shipments is what governs feasibility.

## 2. Full-truckload charge

If inventory costs are small enough relative to transport costs, then a single shipment will always be comprised of an entire full truckload (FTL), so that $q = q_{\max}$. In other situations, it is also likely that a consolidated load comprised of many different shipments, each with a different cube and weight, will only be transported as a full truckload (e.g., many big-box retailers only transport full truckloads from a DC to a store). In this case, although the different shipments could be combined into a single aggregate shipment, it is often more convenient to determine the transport rate for each shipment per ton-mile assuming that $r$ is allocated to the product based on its maximum payload, the FTL rate (\$/ton-mi):

$$
r_{FTL} = \frac{r}{q_{\max}}
\tag{4}
$$

### 2.1 FTL transport cost

The FTL transport cost (\$/yr) is

$$
TC_{FTL} = f\,r_{FTL}\,d = n\,r\,d = w\,d
\tag{5}
$$

where

- $w$ = monetary weight (\$/mi)
- $r$ = TL revenue per loaded truck-mile (\$/mi)
- $d$ = road distance (mi).

When it is reasonable to assume that a shipment will always be transported along with other shipments as part of a full truckload, then using $r_{FTL}$ as the truckload transport rate for the shipment allows its transport cost to be considered in a location decision without having to know the exact mix of other shipments being transported (and the mix, size, and timing can change with each shipment without impacting the decision since only $f$, the annual demand, is used in the analysis) and its cost per mile for transport is independent of shipment size and distance. The formulation using $w$ is useful in location analysis where $w$ corresponds to the criterion used for the minisum transport-oriented single-facility location problem. The two forms of Eq. 5 give the same result: the FTL rate in dollars per ton-mile times the tons and the distance, or the number of truckloads times the rate per truckload-mile times the distance. Either product, $f\,r_{FTL}$ or $n\,r$, is the monetary weight $w$ of the Location lectures, so this is how the details of a particular product to be transported are translated into the monetary weight a location problem needs.

Example 1(c): Annual FTL transport cost

Determine the annual full-truckload transport cost.

```julia
# Code block 3: FTL rate and annual FTL transport cost
d = 532                            # mi, Google Maps road distance
ppiTL = 131.0                      # TL PPI for Jan 2018
@show rTL = 2.00ppiTL/102.7        # $/mi
@show rFTL = rTL/qmax              # $/ton-mi
@show TC_FTL = n * rTL * d         # $/yr
```

```text
rTL = (2.0ppiTL) / 102.7 = 2.5511197663096397
rFTL = rTL / qmax = 0.4174559617597592
TC_FTL = n * rTL * d = 4441.731433123838
```

```text
4441.731433123838
```

$r_{FTL} =$ \$0.4175/ton-mi, so $TC_{FTL} =$ \$4,441.73/yr.

The FTL cost alone does not show whether shipping full truckloads was a good idea. That is the silo problem of organizations in which people are evaluated on their own subgroup. From a transport point of view a shipment would always go full truckload: a manager whose bonus depends on what the company spends on transport would require every shipment to be a full truckload, since that maximizes the utilization of each truck and gives the minimum number of trucks per year. The downside for the company falls on whoever runs the warehouse and is evaluated on its cost. One full truckload may be five years’ usage of some washer, and that inventory has to be insured, heated and air-conditioned, so the warehouse’s costs go through the roof, and from that side the preference is to order just what is needed, in LTL shipments. Many companies still have not integrated the two, although IT systems such as SAP that control several parts of an organization help, since once a decision is built into the software much of the politics drops out. This is the classic trade-off between transport and inventory, the more general name for the warehousing side, since inventory does not have to be in a warehouse. The piece still missing is the inventory side of the ledger.

### 2.2 Interval constraint

Another means of indirectly accounting for inventory costs when assuming full-truckload shipments is to place an upper limit on the average shipment interval. If $t_{\max}$ is the maximum shipment interval, then the FTL shipment size is the lesser of the following, the FTL rate with shipment interval constraint (\$/ton-mi):

$$
r_{FTL} = \frac{r}{\min\bigl\{ f\,t_{\max},\, q_{\max} \bigr\}}
\tag{6}
$$

where

- $t_{\max}$ = maximum shipment interval (yr/TL).

An interval constraint is a poor man’s version of including the inventory cost. Without getting into the details of exactly what the inventory costs are, a shipper may simply want deliveries every week or two because things are changing so much, rather than guess at what will be needed over the next six weeks: six weeks might be the optimum, but the shipper is willing to pay a little more to ship more frequently. An interval constraint also captures multi-stop routing. The reason is that multiple products might each have a different interval on their own, but when they are shipped together on the same truck in multi-stop routing, a single interval constraint is the best compromise among them. Everything here considers only point-to-point shipments, which is limiting, and it makes more sense for a vehicle to stop at several customers along a route, which is the subject of the routing lectures, Lectures 5.1 to 5.3. The only way to evaluate the impact of an interval constraint is to put it into the total logistics cost.

Full truckloads are often a matter of bargaining with the warehouse manager. The full-truckload interval in Ex. 1(b) was about 111 days, and three months is 90 days, so a common compromise is to switch from a truck every 111 days to one every three months. The question is then the impact: how much would the transport cost increase?

Example 1(d): FTL cost with a three-month interval

Determine the cost if the shipments were to be made at least every three months.

A three-month maximum interval sets a minimum frequency, and the transport cost follows from the larger of the two frequencies:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{\max} &= \frac{3}{12} \text{ yr/TL} \;\Rightarrow\; n_{\min} = \frac{1}{t_{\max}} \text{ TL/yr} \;\Rightarrow\; q = \frac{f}{\max\{n,\, n_{\min}\}} \\
TC'_{FTL} &= \max\{n,\, n_{\min}\}\, r\, d
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
$$

where

- $n_{\min}$ = minimum shipment frequency (TL/yr)
- $TC'_{FTL}$ = FTL transport cost under the interval constraint (\$/yr).

Shipping every three months needs about four truckloads a year against the 3.27 being shipped, so the cost will go up; the question is by how much. Three months is one quarter of a year, so a minimum of four truckloads a year is needed, and the shipment size follows from the demand and the larger of the two frequencies. The maximum is there for other problems. Here the number of full truckloads is less than four, but if demand were high enough that five or six full truckloads were already being shipped each year, the minimum of four would not dominate and the cost would not increase, since shipments would already be more frequent than every three months. The maximum handles the case where $n$ is already greater than $n_{\min}$.

```julia
# Code block 4: FTL cost with a three-month interval
@show tmax = 3/12                  # yr/TL
@show nmin = 1/tmax                # TL/yr
@show q = f/max(n, nmin)           # ton
@show TC′_FTL = max(n, nmin) * rTL * d   # $/yr
```

```text
tmax = 3 / 12 = 0.25
nmin = 1 / tmax = 4.0
q = f / max(n, nmin) = 5.0
TC′_FTL = max(n, nmin) * rTL * d = 5428.782862706913
```

```text
5428.782862706913
```

$q =$ 5.0 ton, so $TC'_{FTL} =$ \$5,428.78/yr, \$987.05 a year more than full truckloads.

The engineer’s role, when the transport and warehouse managers are arguing and the warehouse manager wants 90-day shipments, is to answer what it will cost in additional transport: for this product, about \$1,000 a year. That number is then one piece of whatever negotiation takes place inside the company, and without the bigger picture there is no knowing whether the change is a good or a bad decision. This course is not focused on high-level strategic managerial decisions, but instead provides the modeling so that the decision process can incorporate realistic factors into the decision. Previously, because of computational friction, there was never time to get up from the engine room to the bridge to help with navigation: just getting the engines working and keeping them working was the problem. The course is still primarily focused on modeling these low-level, computationally focused details, but with AI it is possible to include more big-picture managerial issues in the analysis. In some sense, the analysis needs to work with the high level and not be stuck in the engine room.

### 2.3 Range of transport charges

One thing about the full truckload is unrealistic: for many products, nobody wants a full truckload of widgets. A supplier typically makes not one product but dozens, so it makes more sense to put large aggregates of several products onto a truck than to ship products individually. The truck may still go out full, but that full truckload is mixed with many other products, so from any one product’s point of view it is an allocated full truckload. The subscript zero in $c_0$ means independent, whether LTL or truckload: the product is not mixed with any other, and that charge is the upper bound, the most that would ever be paid. It applies to a supplier somewhere in northern Canada making one product, with nothing nearby that could be combined onto a truck. Coming south into the United States, almost every state has many other companies and suppliers, and carriers with trucks available, so a dedicated truck is almost never needed and some mixing with other products is possible. The best case is to fill the truck exactly, shipping allocated full truckloads, and that is a lower bound on the cost. The actual cost is likely to fall somewhere in between.

Fig. 1 shows the range of possible transport charges for a single shipment. The independent-shipment charge ($c_0$ via the formula of Lecture 3.2, Sec. 4.3) corresponds to the maximum charge, while the full-truckload charge ($c_{FTL} = r_{FTL}\,q\,d$) corresponds to the minimum likely charge. When multiple shipments are carried on a single truck as part of a consolidated load, each shipment’s charge corresponds to an allocated portion of the total transport charge and is represented in the figure as any of the charges between the independent and full-truckload charges. The consolidated charge approaches the full-truckload charge as the load reaches truck capacity. All of the charges are the same at the maximum payload. Note also that an allocated charge can be less than the minimum charge for an independent shipment. For a shipment of at most one truckload, the two bounds are:

$$
q \leq q_{\max} \;\Rightarrow\; [\, UB ,\, LB \,] = \bigl[\, c_{0}(q) ,\; q\, r_{FTL}\, d \,\bigr]
\tag{8}
$$

where

- $UB$ = largest likely charge at size $q$ (\$)
- $LB$ = smallest likely charge at size $q$ (\$).

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
ppiLTL = 177.4                     # LTL PPI for Jan 2018, as in 3.2
cTLh(q)  = charge_tl(q, s, d; r = rTL, Kwt = Kwt,
                     Kcu = Kcu, ppi = ppiTL)
cLTLh(q) = charge_ltl(q, s, d; ppi = ppiLTL)
c0(q)    = min(cTLh(q), cLTLh(q))  # independent charge, the upper bound
cFTL(q)  = rFTL*q*d                # allocated full-truckload, the lower

# The TL/LTL indifference point, searched only up to the LTL
# estimate's cube bound of 650 ft^3.
qLTLmax = 650s/2000
qI = optimize(q -> abs(cTLh(q) - cLTLh(q)), 0.075, qLTLmax).minimizer
MC_LTL = mincharge_ltl(d; ppi = ppiLTL)

# A split horizontal axis: the first 1.5 tons take 45% of the width,
# the rest out to two and a half truckloads the other 55%, linear
# inside each piece.
QSPLIT, QEND = 1.5, 2.5qmax
u(q) = q <= QSPLIT ? 0.45q/QSPLIT :
       0.45 + 0.55(q - QSPLIT)/(QEND - QSPLIT)

blue   = RGBf(0.13, 0.35, 0.60)
purple = RGBf(0.58, 0.20, 0.72)
red    = RGBf(0.85, 0.10, 0.10)
olive  = RGBf(0.40, 0.48, 0.20)

fig = Figure(size = (687, 480))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1];
          xlabel = "Shipment size (ton)",
          ylabel = "Transport charge (\$)",
          title = "Transport charge for a shipment",
          titlesize = 17, xlabelsize = 16, ylabelsize = 16,
          xticklabelsize = 14, yticklabelsize = 14)
vlines!(ax, [u(QSPLIT)]; color = (:black, 0.45), linewidth = 1.2,
        linestyle = :dashdot)
qs = range(1/2000, QEND; length = 4000)
lines!(ax, u.(qs), cFTL.(qs); color = purple, linewidth = 2.6)
# Dotted: LTL past the indifference point, and the one-truckload
# charge short of it.
qL = range(qI, qLTLmax; length = 200)
lines!(ax, u.(qL), cLTLh.(qL); color = blue, linewidth = 1.6,
       linestyle = :dot)
lines!(ax, [0, u(qI)], [rTL*d, rTL*d]; color = blue, linewidth = 1.6,
       linestyle = :dot)
lines!(ax, u.(qs), c0.(qs); color = blue, linewidth = 2.6)

# Both axes start at zero, so the origin sits in the corner. The limits
# and ticks come before the labels, because a label set along a curve
# takes the curve's angle as drawn, and that depends on both.
xlims!(ax, 0, 1)
ylims!(ax, 0, 1.1*3rTL*d)
ax.xticks = (u.([150/2000, qI, qmax, 2qmax]),
             ["150/2000", @sprintf("%.4f", qI),
              @sprintf("%.2f", qmax), @sprintf("%.2f", 2qmax)])
# The LTL minimum charge (MC) is named on its own tick: the floor it
# labels is too short for a label inside the plot to clear the curve.
ax.yticks = ([MC_LTL, rTL*d, 2rTL*d, 3rTL*d],
             ["MC " * @sprintf("%.2f", MC_LTL);
              string.(round.(Int, (1:3) .* rTL*d))])

# The angle of a curve on the page, measured in pixels between two of
# its points, so that a label rotated to it runs parallel to the curve.
function page_angle(c, q1, q2)
    p1 = Makie.project(ax.scene, :data, :pixel, Point3f(u(q1), c(q1), 0))
    p2 = Makie.project(ax.scene, :data, :pixel, Point3f(u(q2), c(q2), 0))
    return atan(p2[2] - p1[2], p2[1] - p1[1])
end
```

Figure 1: Transport charge for a shipment. The independent charge (blue) is the upper bound: floored at the LTL minimum charge (MC), LTL to the indifference point, then one, two and three truckloads. The allocated full-truckload charge (purple) is the lower bound, and the allocated truckload charge of a shipment carried in a consolidated load lies between the two. The horizontal axis is split at 1.5 tons, marked by the labeled dash-dot rule, so that the LTL branch has room to show its shape; the purple line bends there only because the scale changes.

The purple line is probably never achieved exactly, since that would take a perfectly full truck. Nor does the shipper have to pay the independent charge, which is what hiring the whole truck costs, paid for whether it is filled or not. What is paid falls somewhere in the range between, and that is the allocated truckload charge. The point of all of this is negotiating with the carrier. The independent charge for the shipment could already be calculated; now the allocated full-truckload charge can be too. It is the lower bound, below which the charge is unlikely to go, and the independent charge is the most that should be paid, so a shipper negotiating with a carrier can try to settle on something in the middle. That is the range of negotiation.

So far there are two possibilities: ship full truckloads, or put a restriction such as a time interval constraint on them, as with shipments every three months. The question is always whether three months is the best: would shipping every two months be better? The way to make it a real decision is to look at it from an inventory perspective.

## 3. Inventory cost

Inventory is taken up in more detail at the end of the course, but some of it is needed now. Inventory can be viewed as a contrast between its role and its position in a supply chain.

### 3.1 Total logistics cost

Total logistics costs are any of the relevant costs associated with providing a logistics service, where a relevant cost is a cost that differs when comparing multiple alternatives and, as such, can be used in making a decision between the alternatives. Total logistics cost decomposes into three such terms, and its inventory cost into one term for each role that inventory plays:

$$
\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC}{TLC}}\mathllap{TLC} = \mathrlap{TC + IC + PC}\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC_\text{working} + IC_\text{economic} + IC_\text{safety}}{TC + IC + PC}} \tag{9}
$$

$$
\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC}{TLC}}\mathllap{IC} = \mathrlap{IC_\text{working} + IC_\text{economic} + IC_\text{safety}}\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC_\text{working} + IC_\text{economic} + IC_\text{safety}}{TC + IC + PC}} \tag{10}
$$

where

- $TC$ = transport cost (\$/yr)
- $IC$ = inventory cost (\$/yr)
- $PC$ = purchase cost (\$/yr)
- $IC_\text{working}$ = cost of working stock (\$/yr)
- $IC_\text{economic}$ = cost of economic stock (\$/yr)
- $IC_\text{safety}$ = cost of safety stock (\$/yr).

With respect to transportation, there is almost always a transportation cost component of total logistics cost even for a single origin and destination, since differences in the speed and reliability of transport affect cost. Since it is usually not economic to ship individual units of an item, multiple units are batched together in a single shipment, and unless they are used immediately, those batched units incur an inventory cost for storage while they are consumed. The cost to purchase items can differ if different suppliers are considered, and typically a lower purchase cost for an item is associated with a higher transport cost. Inventory is classified along two independent axes: role (why it is held) and position (where it sits in the materials flow). Any role can occur at any position; Table 1 gives, for each role, why it is held and what it is at each position.

Table 1: Inventory by role and position: why each role is held, and what it is at each position in the materials flow, from raw material through work in process to finished goods.

| Role | Why it is held | Position | What it is there |
|---|---|---|---|
| Working stock | to allow production, including transport | Raw material | in transit from supplier |
| Work in process | queuing between operations | | |
| Finished goods | in transit to customers, or presentation stock | | |
| Economic stock | to make purchasing or production cheaper | Raw material | cycle stock from truckloads |
| Work in process | batches spreading setup cost | | |
| Finished goods | seasonal pre-build | | |
| Safety stock | to buffer uncertainty | Raw material | buffer against supplier delay |
| Work in process | buffer between operations | | |
| Finished goods | buffer against uncertain demand | | |

Working stock is held as part of the production process, with transportation viewed as a production process. Product on a ship coming from China is in-transit inventory, and somebody has to finance it even though it is sitting in a container on a ship. Safety stock covers anything that is not perfect; in the models of this lecture everything is assumed perfectly constant, like clockwork, with no uncertainty, which is not realistic, and accounting for uncertainty is what safety stock does, the subject of Lectures 6.1 and 6.2. This lecture considers only economic stock. Even in a perfect world, freight is lumpy and there are scale economies that make shipping larger units advantageous, and that is cycle stock, the only kind of inventory dealt with in this lecture.

NoteWorking and safety stock in transport

Working stock is what decides between air cargo and ocean. From Singapore, air takes a day or two and a ship a couple of weeks, and the trade-off depends on the value: millions of dollars of high-end textiles fit on one cargo plane, so even at many times the cost of ocean, the cost of financing that inventory for two weeks would probably make air cargo preferable. For the choice of mode, the in-transit inventory cost is probably the main driver.

In transport, safety stock is not only stock kept on hand just in case. A construction site installing a large air-conditioning unit next Tuesday could have it arrive Tuesday morning, which would minimize transport cost, but more realistically it would arrive a few days early in case of disruptions, and financing a \$10 million unit for those extra two or three days is safety stock, even for a one-time shipment. In transport, safety stock is often a matter of when a shipment is scheduled to arrive: a drive that normally takes 30 minutes but occasionally an hour means leaving an hour early most days, and the extra 30 minutes of arriving early on average is a kind of safety stock of earliness.

Total logistics cost is, in effect, all costs that could change as a result of a logistics-related decision: the transport cost and an inventory cost that can include all three roles. The same unit of inventory often serves several purposes. An item that arrived early because of uncertainty in delivery time is safety stock, but it also arrived in a bigger quantity for economic reasons, so the roles combine and cannot simply be separated and added together. Purchase cost enters as a question of who, since there is often a sourcing option: a domestic supplier might charge \$100 per unit and an overseas one \$60. That is better from a purchase point of view, but what matters is the landed cost of getting the product to where it is needed, which adds the freight transport and the inventory cost of, say, two weeks on a ship. With just one supplier, purchase cost is a fixed quantity and not part of total logistics cost; when there are options, it can be part of the equation. For periodic truck shipments the focus is on cycle stock, which is the most realistic case for trucking. Transit times differ by only a day or two, so unless the product is worth millions of dollars, the difference in working, in-transit stock is insignificant. And a truckload arrives 12 hours after it leaves, without going from 12 hours to 48 even if the truck breaks down, since another tractor can replace it, so trucking carries little of the uncertainty that safety stock covers; rail carries more, and ocean shipping much more, as the strike that closed the East and Gulf Coast ports for three days in October 2024 showed1. Purchase cost can still differ, between two domestic suppliers or, for an overseas one, in the trucking from the port against from a domestic supplier. Cycle stock and purchase cost are the two factors for trucking.

So total logistics cost is not a single term. It is an umbrella term for whatever factors are important to the decision being made: transport and inventory cost always, and purchase cost when two suppliers, perhaps one overseas and one domestic, would charge different prices.

### 3.2 Cycle inventory

The annual cost of cycle inventory is the annual cost of holding one ton times the average annual inventory level:

$$
IC_\text{cycle} \;=\; \underbrace{vh}_{\text{cost of holding 1 ton 1 yr}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{\alpha q}_{\text{average inventory level}}
\tag{11}
$$

where

- $v$ = unit value of shipment (\$/ton)
- $h$ = inventory carrying rate, the cost per dollar of inventory per year (1/yr)
- $q$ = shipment size (ton)
- $\alpha$ = average inter-shipment inventory fraction at origin and destination.

The cost of holding one ton of inventory for one year is $vh$ (\$/ton-yr). The inventory carrying rate is expressed as a fraction since the cost per dollar of inventory per year (\$/\$/yr) reduces to 1/yr. This is highly formalized and is used throughout the course, with the same standard terminology. The unit value $v$ is in dollars per ton; other units are possible, but tons are convenient. Besides being convenient, tons are the default unit for most freight transport and throughout the course, except for the very smallest shipments, package express and air freight, which are weighed in pounds or kilograms2. The carrying rate $h$ is in dollars per dollar of inventory per year, so the dollars cancel and its units are one over a year, and the product $vh$ is in dollars per ton-year. That is multiplied by the fraction $\alpha$, which is 1 here for a reason given in Sec. 3.4, and by the shipment size $q$ in tons, so the tons cancel and $IC_\text{cycle}$ is in dollars per year. Unit analysis is always important. Total logistics cost is the sum of the transport cost, the inventory cost and, where it applies, the purchase cost, all in dollars per year, so it is encouraging that the inventory cost works out in those units.

The value for $v$ can be determined from the purchase price or production cost. That is, $v$ is on a cost basis: what it is costing the company to keep the product in inventory, not the opportunity cost of selling the product for a higher value.

### 3.3 Carrying rate

Components of $h$ are interest, warehousing, and obsolescence:

$$
h = \text{interest} + \text{warehousing} + \text{obsolescence}, \tag{12}
$$

where the interest (5%) and warehousing (6%)3 rates are the financial-cost and storage rows of Table 2 in Lecture 3.1, each as a fraction of the \$3,202 billion of total U.S. inventory, and so averages over everything from sand to high-tech computer products, and the obsolescence component, which is what really drives cycle stock since it differs a lot between products, follows from the default yearly rate for a manufactured product, which Table 3 in Lecture 3.2 puts at 25–30% for general durable manufactured goods, $h = 0.3 \Rightarrow h_\text{obs} \approx 0.2$.

A good rule of thumb for most manufactured products, whatever kind of widgets they are, is about 20% for obsolescence and about 10% for interest and warehousing together, so for a manufactured product with no more detail, $h$ of about 0.3 is a good default value, and it is usually pretty robust. For a widget or any kind of discrete manufactured product, when no rate is given, 0.3 is the value to use. Working as a logistics engineer, nobody typically gives these numbers, so it is good practice to decide what would be reasonable: for data not immediately available, whether a study is needed or a reasonable default value will do as a first cut. That is why default values, the design constants of Lecture 3.2, matter: the idea is to get a result quickly.

For most items, interest and warehousing costs are fairly constant while obsolescence cost can differ significantly between items. For a product with a low finished-goods inventory (FGI) cost, measured on a yearly scale, $h = h_\text{int} + h_\text{wh} + h_\text{obs}$. For a product with a high FGI cost, measured on an hourly scale, $h \approx h_\text{obs}$ and interest and warehousing can be ignored, since $(h_\text{int} + h_\text{wh})/H = (0.05 + 0.06)/2000 = 0.000055$, where $H$ is the number of operating hours per year.

For products with a low finished-goods inventory cost, handled on a yearly basis, $h$ really is the sum of the three components: obsolescence can be the biggest, but the other two are still significant. For items with a high finished-goods inventory cost, $h$ is essentially the obsolescence cost alone, and interest and warehousing can be ignored, because the product degrades significantly on an hourly basis. Ice degrades almost 100% in 30 minutes unless it is refrigerated, and food is another example: a \$50 restaurant meal produced ahead for efficiency and kept under a lamp has a crazy inventory cost. The same formulas that apply to manufactured products apply to food, and they say how bananas should be shipped. When the 2024 strike closed the East and Gulf Coast ports, bananas were among the first products expected to run short, since more than three quarters of U.S. bananas arrive through those ports4. Much else could be sourced through the West Coast: apples can be stored for a long time, so they could come in through Oakland instead of Savannah, but bananas cannot take that route to serve Raleigh because their obsolescence is so significant. Sand is the other extreme, where nothing goes obsolete and $h$ might be 2% or 5%; bananas are at the far end. For some products the cost of obsolescence can overwhelm both the interest and the warehousing portions, and for a product with a high finished-goods inventory cost, inventory might be measured in hours: the question is not the inventory cost per year but the cost per hour. Fries at a restaurant that have to be thrown out after 20 or 30 minutes in the hopper are an example; whatever it cost to make them, their inventory is measured in minutes. Depending on how perishable a product is, its obsolescence cost can be very high.

The obsolescence component $h_\text{obs}$ can be estimated using the “percent-reduction interval” method: given the time $t_h$ at which a product loses $x_h$-percent of its original value $v$, it follows that:

$$
\begin{gathered}
h_\text{obs}\,t_h\,v = x_h\,v \;\Rightarrow\; h_\text{obs}\,t_h = x_h \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{h_\text{obs} = \frac{x_h}{t_h}}, \\
\text{and } t_h = \frac{x_h}{h_\text{obs}}
\end{gathered}
\tag{13}
$$

where

- $h_\text{obs}$ = obsolescence component of the carrying rate (1/yr, or 1/hr)
- $t_h$ = time after which the product has lost $x_h$ of its value (yr, or the same unit of time)
- $x_h$ = fraction of the original value lost (dimensionless).

In practical terms, bananas lose 80% or even 100% of their value after one week, and another product might lose half its value after three months, or 20% after two months. Framing it that way is useful because somebody in industry can usually answer a question such as how much the product could be sold for after some number of weeks, and those two pieces of information translate into the equivalent effective obsolescence cost. It is important that $t_h$ be in the same time units as $t_{CT}$, the cycle time of Lecture 1.3.

For example, if a product loses 80% of its value after 2 hours 40 minutes:

$$
t_h = 2 + \frac{40}{60} = 2.67~\text{hr} \;\Rightarrow\; h = \frac{x_h}{t_h} = \frac{0.8}{2.67} = 0.3.
$$

It is probably not food, since two hours and 40 minutes is too long, but in certain service industries something could be worth only 20% of its original value after that time. With the time as 2.67 hours, $h$ is 0.3, and that is 0.3 on an hourly basis. Including interest and warehousing would make it 0.300055, which makes no difference, so obsolescence alone is the value to use for $h$. It can then be put into the total logistics cost to get sensible decisions about operating on an hourly, daily, weekly or any other basis, provided the time unit is the same as that of the activity.

### 3.4 Inventory fraction

Since demand is constant throughout the year, one half of a shipment is stored at the destination, on average. Assuming that the production rate is also constant, one half of a shipment will also be stored at the origin, on average. So $\alpha = \alpha_O + \alpha_D = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1$, the average annual inventory level that Fig. 2 draws for three successive shipments. Fig. 3 draws all four production–consumption regimes with $\alpha_O$ and $\alpha_D$ marked on each, and Table 2 collects the resulting $\alpha$. In the constant-production case, as soon as the truck delivering the last shipment has left the production facility, the inventory there is at zero. The facility then produces at a constant rate until the inventory reaches the quantity to be shipped, $q$, at which point the truck picks it up and it is in transit. At the destination, the inventory was zero the instant before the truck arrived, is $q$ once it is dropped off, and then goes down at a constant rate to zero, when the next truck arrives. Over successive shipments everything lines up: the origin goes from zero to $q$ and immediately back to zero, again and again, and the destination starts at $q$ and goes down to zero as each truck arrives. With everything drawn as straight lines, the average at each end is $q/2$. The average inventory level is then $q/2$ at the origin plus $q/2$ at the destination, one half plus one half times $q$, and the two together give the value of 1 used for $\alpha$.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
axs = [Axis(fig[k, 1]) for k in 1:3]
for (k, axk) in enumerate(axs)
    # t0, not s: a name assigned in a top-level loop is the global one,
    # and s is the product's density.

    hidedecorations!(axk); hidespines!(axk)
    # the time axis, with an arrowhead

           linewidth = 2.6)

end
# The first row carries the labels.

      fontsize = 17, offset = (0, 12))

         orientation = :down, fontsize = 15, color = ink,
         textcolor = ink)

      fontsize = 16)

      align = (:center, :top), fontsize = 16)
```

Figure 2: Average annual inventory level with constant production and constant consumption, for three successive shipments. Each shipment builds at the origin from 0 to $q$ while it is produced, is in transit, and is drawn down at the destination from $q$ to 0 while it is consumed, so the average at each end is $q/2$.

From Fig. 2, the average annual inventory level is

$$
\frac{q}{2} + \frac{q}{2} = \left( \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \right) q = (1)\, q \Rightarrow \alpha = 1
\tag{14}
$$

The four inter-shipment inventory fraction alternatives in Fig. 3 each add a fraction held at the origin to one held at the destination:

$$
\alpha = \alpha_{O} + \alpha_{D}
\tag{15}
$$

where

- $\alpha_O$ = part of $\alpha$ held at the origin (dimensionless)
- $\alpha_D$ = part of $\alpha$ held at the destination (dimensionless).

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# One regime: how the origin builds a shipment, how the destination
# uses it, and the average (dashed) at each end.
function regime!(axr, prod, cons)
    hidedecorations!(axr); hidespines!(axr)
    lines!(axr, [0, 1.02], [0, 0]; color = ink, linewidth = 2.5)
    scatter!(axr, [1.02], [0]; marker = :rtriangle, markersize = 14,
             color = ink)
    if prod == :constant           # builds steadily over the cycle
        lines!(axr, [0, 0.4], [0, 1]; color = blue, linewidth = 2.6)
        lines!(axr, [0, 0.4], [0.5, 0.5]; color = red, linewidth = 2,
               linestyle = :dash)
        text!(axr, 0, 0.5; text = L"\frac{q}{2}",
              align = (:right, :center), fontsize = 16, offset = (-4, 0))
    else                           # made in one short batch before pickup
        lines!(axr, [0, 0.35], [0.015, 0.015]; color = red,
               linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash)
        lines!(axr, [0.35, 0.4], [0, 1]; color = blue, linewidth = 2.6)
        text!(axr, 0, 0.015; text = L"\approx 0",
              align = (:right, :bottom), fontsize = 16, offset = (-2, 2))
    end
    if cons == :constant           # drawn down steadily over the cycle
        lines!(axr, [0.56, 0.96], [1, 0]; color = blue, linewidth = 2.6)
        lines!(axr, [0.56, 0.96], [0.5, 0.5]; color = red, linewidth = 2,
               linestyle = :dash)
        text!(axr, 0.96, 0.5; text = L"\frac{q}{2}",
              align = (:left, :center), fontsize = 16, offset = (4, 0))
    else                           # used as soon as it arrives
        lines!(axr, [0.56, 0.61], [1, 0]; color = blue, linewidth = 2.6)
        lines!(axr, [0.61, 0.96], [0.015, 0.015]; color = red,
               linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash)
        text!(axr, 0.96, 0.015; text = L"\approx 0",
              align = (:left, :bottom), fontsize = 16, offset = (2, 2))
    end
    text!(axr, 0.2, -0.06; text = "$(titlecase(string(prod))) production",
          align = (:center, :top), fontsize = 14)
    text!(axr, 0.78, -0.06;
          text = cons == :constant ? "Constant consumption" :
                                     "Immediate consumption",
          align = (:center, :top), fontsize = 14)
    xlims!(axr, -0.14, 1.12); ylims!(axr, -0.3, 1.05)
    return axr
end

fig = Figure(size = (687, 470))
cases = [(:constant, :constant,
          L"\alpha = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1"),
         (:constant, :immediate,
          L"\alpha = \frac{1}{2} + 0 = \frac{1}{2}"),
         (:batch, :constant,
          L"\alpha = 0 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}"),
         (:batch, :immediate, L"\alpha = 0 + 0 = 0")]
for (i, (p, c, lab)) in enumerate(cases)
    regime!(Axis(fig[fld1(i, 2), mod1(i, 2)]; title = lab,
                 titlesize = 17), p, c)
end
fig
```

Figure 3: Inter-shipment inventory fraction alternatives. Constant production holds $q/2$ at the origin on average and batch production almost nothing; constant consumption holds $q/2$ at the destination and immediate consumption almost nothing.

Table 2: Inventory fraction $\alpha$ for the four production–consumption regimes.

| Regime | $\alpha_O$ | $\alpha_D$ | $\alpha$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Constant production / constant consumption | ½ | ½ | 1 |
| Constant production / immediate consumption | ½ | 0 | ½ |
| Batch production / constant consumption | 0 | ½ | ½ |
| Batch production / immediate consumption | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Constant production is not terribly realistic. Most companies are not dedicated to producing a single product for a single customer; more realistically they do batch production, with many different customers, and produce any one customer’s product over a really short period of time, so there is almost zero inventory at the origin. With a two-month shipping interval, for example, instead of producing at a constant rate over two months they might produce for one or two days, which is essentially zero. With batch production and constant consumption, $\alpha$ is zero plus one half, or one half. A problem will not say to use an $\alpha$ of 0.5; it will say that production occurs in batches at the supplier and consumption is constant at the destination, and that is what indicates an $\alpha$ of one half. Constant production would take a dedicated production line, such as an auto supplier near Spartanburg that supplies only BMW, and even then it is possible but not likely. Batch production with constant consumption is the typical case for most manufacturing.

Batch production with immediate consumption would fit, for example, a company that builds large HVAC systems and ships them to commercial construction sites all over the country: it would produce in batches, load the truck and ship, and each system, arriving perhaps a little early as safety stock against uncertainty, would be installed immediately. Inventory would be almost zero and play no part, since inventory only becomes an issue when stock is on hand over a long period of time.

Dedicated production and consumption is also unlikely to be practical for another reason: with both dedicated, why not co-locate them and not bother with transport at all? The usual reason for going to the trouble of transporting a product is to produce batches of many different products in one location, with economies of scale and much more efficiently, and then transport them to the many locations where customers consume them at a constant rate. That is why batch production with constant consumption is the most common case.

It could be argued that a shipper does not pay a supplier’s inventory cost, so that with constant production at the supplier the inventory held there is of no concern. But, as with the free-on-board argument of Lecture 2.2, Sec. 2, about who actually pays the transport cost, it all comes out in the wash as a first approximation: the supplier has to carry that inventory and make money, so the shipper pays for it indirectly in a higher cost for the product, even though it is not a line item in the budget. In a calculation it is a good idea to include the origin’s inventory cost as if the shipper were paying it directly.

NoteOther regimes for $\alpha$

The parameter $\alpha$ denotes the average fraction of the shipment size q that is held, in total, across the origin and the destination. For example, assuming that, on an annual basis, the supply and demand rates between a given O-D pair are constant, then, for a shipment of size q, the expected cycle inventory is $q/2$ at each end,5 meaning that the total cycle inventory across the origin and the destination is q and, therefore, $\alpha = 1$; also, if supply is not constant (e.g., batch production) but the time of production is not coordinated with the time of shipment, then $\alpha = 1$ (assuming production is equally likely to have occurred at anytime between shipments). If production at the origin is instantaneous, with a constant demand rate at the destination (i.e., the traditional EOQ model), then $\alpha = 0.5$. If, however, both production and consumption are instantaneous, then $\alpha = 0$ (more on this case below). Finally, if the supplier is another firm and there are no negotiations with the supplier, e.g., to share the benefits of using an optimal shipment size that accounts for the supplier’s inventory costs, then (from the point of view of the shipper-customer) $\alpha = 0.5$. Thus, annual inventory holding costs are given by $\alpha v h q$.

Example 1(e): Cycle inventory cost at FTL

Give a reasonable estimate for the total annual cycle inventory cost at the FTL shipment size $q_{\max}$, with $v = \$25{,}000$/ton, $h = 0.3~\text{yr}^{-1}$, and $\alpha = 1$.

The carrying rate of 0.3 comes from the product losing 5 percent of its value after 3 months, which, with the average values for interest on funds and for warehousing, makes it approximately 0.3; almost 20% of it is the obsolescence factor. The example assumes constant production and constant consumption, so $\alpha$ is 1, and the carrying rate is the estimate for a manufactured product. Table 2 in Lecture 3.1 put the average for the entire United States at about 16%, but that includes a lot of low-value construction products, so 16% is the average for everything and not the rate to use. A product known to be manufactured is typically of much higher value, and 0.3 is a good estimate.

```julia
v = 25000                          # $/ton
h = 0.3                            # 1/yr
@show IC_FTL = α*v*h*qmax          # $/yr
```

Example 1(f): Total logistics cost at FTL

Combine the transport and inventory costs to obtain the annual total logistics cost (TLC) for full-truckload TL shipments.

The total logistics cost of full truckloads is the sum of the two:

$$
TLC_{FTL} = TC_{FTL} + IC_{\text{cycle}} = n\, r\, d + \alpha v h q
\tag{16}
$$

where

- $TLC_{FTL}$ = total logistics cost of FTL shipments (\$/yr).

```julia
# Code block 6: total logistics cost at FTL
@show TC_FTL                       # $/yr
@show IC_FTL                       # $/yr
@show TLC_FTL = TC_FTL + IC_FTL    # $/yr
```

```text
TC_FTL = 4441.731433123838
IC_FTL = 45833.333333333336
TLC_FTL = TC_FTL + IC_FTL = 50275.06476645717
```

```text
50275.06476645717
```

$TLC_{FTL} =$ \$4,441.73 + \$45,833.33 = \$50,275.06/yr.

The inventory cost really dominates, which says that a full truckload is far too large a shipment size. At the optimal truckload size, the transport and inventory costs should be of the same order of magnitude, right in the same ballpark if not exactly the same, and when they are exactly the same the size is optimal. Ignoring purchase cost, the total logistics cost is around \$50,000. The question is whether it can be done better, rather than stopping here, and what engineers like to do is optimize.

## 4. Optimal shipment size

Transport costs typically decrease with increasing size due to economies of scale associated with providing the transport, while inventory costs increase since more inventory is held when shipment size increases. The optimal shipment size corresponds to the size that minimizes the sum of transport and inventory costs. Selecting the shipment size on the basis of its TLC requires that both inventory carrying and transportation costs be specified as a function of $q$. Considering only cycle inventory costs,

$$
TLC(q) = TC(q) + IC(q) = \frac{f}{q}\,c(q) + \alpha v h q,
\tag{17}
$$

with $\alpha$, $v$, and $h$ as defined above. Model 1 states the problem this section solves.

minimize: total logistics cost of transporting a product point-to-point (P2P) periodically, transport plus cycle inventory

solve for:
(a) average shipment size, a positive weight in tons;
(b) service that carries it, TL or LTL.

subject to:
(a) payload: a TL shipment is no larger than one full truckload;
(b) validity: an LTL shipment stays within the range the LTL rate estimate was fitted on.

return: independent shipment size with the lower total logistics cost

assumptions:
(a) annual demand is known and constant;
(b) product value, carrying rate and inventory fraction do not depend on shipment size;
(c) in-transit inventory is the same for TL and LTL, so it is not a relevant cost.

Model 1: Minimum-TLC shipment size

The model returns only the shipment size because the size alone determines the service: with both services evaluated at that size, the selected one always has the lower total logistics cost. The reason is that the selected service’s optimal cost is no more than the other service’s optimal cost, which is no more than what the other service would cost at the returned size, if it can carry that size at all.

### 4.1 TL shipment size

Model 1 is solved one service at a time, and its first formulation is for TL service, where the optimal shipment size has a closed form.

Model 1 formulation: Analytic TL formulation

The total annual logistics cost for TL shipments is given by the sum of the transportation cost (TC) and the cycle inventory costs (IC) at the origin and destination, specifically

$$
TLC_{TL}(q) = \frac{f}{q}\max\bigl\{ c_{TL}, MC_{TL} \bigr\} + \alpha v h q
\approx \frac{f}{q}\, r d + \alpha v h q.
\tag{18}
$$

Minimizing with respect to $q$ yields

$$
q_{TL}^{*} = \min\left\{ \sqrt{\frac{f \max\{ r d, MC_{TL} \}}{\alpha v h}},\;
q_{\max} \right\} \approx \sqrt{\frac{f r d}{\alpha v h}},
\tag{19}
$$

where the approximation ignores the minimum charge and maximum payload restrictions.

- $TLC_{TL}(q)$ = total logistics cost of TL shipments of size $q$ (\$/yr)
- $c_{TL}$ = TL transport charge (\$)
- $MC_{TL}$ = TL minimum charge (\$)
- $q_{TL}^{*}$ = optimal TL shipment size (ton).

For TL shipments the size can be found in closed form. With $q$ in the denominator of the transport term and in the numerator of the inventory term, the standard calculus approach of setting the derivative to zero and solving for $q$ gives a square-root formula. It is the economic order quantity of inventory courses, the same idea that appears anywhere economic stock is calculated, such as the batch size a production line should produce, so it is nothing specific to freight transport: the transport terms are in the numerator and the inventory terms in the denominator. What is interesting, compared with the full truckload, is that distance is a component of the optimal size. As the distance gets smaller the optimal size gets smaller too, and as it goes to zero essentially no cycle stock is carried. That makes sense: a supplier shipping to an auto assembly plant hundreds of miles away wants to utilize its trucks, and as the distance goes to zero the supplier is effectively co-located, in the same facility or across the street. Driving down I-85 through Greenville, the suppliers of the BMW plant line the side of the road, their distance near zero, which makes just-in-time delivery possible. So at least qualitatively the formula moves in the right direction. In a location problem, the optimal quantity is then different at every location; full truckloads are about the only case without that complication.

The practical problem with the square-root formula is that the quantity could in principle go down to a pound, and shipping one pound by truck makes no sense: there is a minimum charge, so the charge relative to distance is replaced by the larger of it and the minimum charge. At the other extreme, a result of 20 tons would be far beyond what a truck can physically carry of the product in Ex. 1: its trailer’s weight capacity is 25 tons, but the product’s cube fills the trailer at $q_{\max} =$ 6.11 tons, so the size is cut off at $q_{\max}$. A proper function includes both restrictions, but as long as the numbers are not extreme, the square-root formula is a good approximation.

Example 1(g): Optimal TL shipment size

Allowing shipment sizes less than a full truckload, determine the TL shipment size $q_{TL}^{*}$ that minimizes the annual TLC for TL service, and the resulting $TLC_{TL}^{*}$.

```julia

@show qᵒTL = sqrt((f*rTL*d)/(α*v*h))   # ton
@show TCᵒ_TL = (f/qᵒTL)*rTL*d          # $/yr
@show ICᵒ_TL = α*v*h*qᵒTL              # $/yr
@show TLCᵒ_TL = TCᵒ_TL + ICᵒ_TL        # $/yr
```

```text
qᵒTL = sqrt((f * rTL * d) / (α * v * h)) = 1.9024165093737864
TCᵒ_TL = (f / qᵒTL) * rTL * d = 14268.123820303399
ICᵒ_TL = α * v * h * qᵒTL = 14268.123820303397
TLCᵒ_TL = TCᵒ_TL + ICᵒ_TL = 28536.247640606794
```

```text
28536.247640606794
```

$q_{TL}^{*} =$ 1.9024 ton, with $TC =$ \$14,268.12 and $IC =$ \$14,268.12, so $TLC_{TL}^{*} =$ \$28,536.25/yr.

The optimal size of about 1.9 tons is a big reduction from the full truckload of 6.11 tons, and with it the transport and inventory costs are each about \$14,200, summing to about \$28,500, just over half the cost of full truckloads. It is not an accident that the two are exactly equal: for this equation, inventory and transport cost are always exactly the same at the optimal solution. That gives a way of knowing how far a solution is from optimal. The big imbalance at full truckloads, about \$4,400 of transport against about \$45,800 of inventory, shows that it is not close to optimal from a truckload point of view; transport and inventory costs close to each other indicate a size close to optimal.

Example 1(h): Allocated FTL

Including the minimum-charge and maximum-payload restrictions, determine the TLC if a shipment of size $q_{TL}^{*}$ could be made as an allocated full-truckload (sharing the truck across many shipments).

Charged at the FTL rate, a shipment of size $q_{TL}^{*}$ costs:

$$
TLC_\text{AllocFTL}(q_{TL}^{*}) \;=\; \frac{f}{q_{TL}^{*}} \bigl(q_{TL}^{*} r_{FTL} d\bigr) + \alpha v h q_{TL}^{*}
\;=\; f \frac{r}{q_{\max}} d + \alpha v h q_{TL}^{*}
\tag{20}
$$

where

- $TLC_\text{AllocFTL}$ = total logistics cost at the allocated FTL charge (\$/yr).

```julia
# Code block 8: TLC as an allocated full truckload
@show TLC_AllocFTL = f*rTL/qmax*d + α*v*h*qᵒTL   # $/yr
```

```text
TLC_AllocFTL = ((f * rTL) / qmax) * d + α * v * h * qᵒTL = 18709.855253427235
```

```text
18709.855253427235
```

$TLC_\text{AllocFTL} =$ \$18,709.86/yr, against \$28,536.25/yr as an independent TL shipment.

The allocated full truckload, about \$18,700, is the lower bound, and the optimal independent truckload, about \$28,500, the upper; in reality the cost would fall somewhere in between. A carrier contacted for this product will not dedicate a truck to it, but will pick it up along with other products from other shippers, so the shipper should not be paying \$28,500 and is unlikely to get \$18,700 either, since the carrier’s truck will not be 100% efficient; a reasonable guess is somewhere around \$22,000 to \$23,000. The equality of transport and inventory cost holds only at the optimal truckload size, not for the allocated charge, which uses that size rather than its own optimum. With the allocated charge the inventory would drive the size down to zero, so the allocated problem is not well formed: its optimum would be to ship one unit at a time, which is never seen in practice. The point to take away is that shipping everything as an independent truckload that occupies 1.9 tons of a truck with a six-ton capacity is not realistic. A recommendation to send trucks out with only a third of their capacity used will not last long, since someone will ask why other products are not added to the truck; that is never a winning game. The reality is to contact a carrier that can mix the product with others. So the independent optimum carries a red star: it keeps the analysis simple, but it is not the end of the game.

NoteWhat the TL model leaves out

Note that in-transit inventory costs are ignored because, for distances greater than one-day’s travel, single-driver TL and LTL transit times are approximately equal (while team drivers can be used for faster TL transit, the cost per mile increases because of the additional labor costs). Also, the increase in value associated with a load reaching its destination, which is at a minimum equal to the cost of transporting the load, is ignored. Finally, for the case discussed above where $\alpha = 0$, total logistics cost consists only of transportation costs, and technically, the value of $q$ that minimizes $TLC_{TL}$ is $q = \infty$; however, by Eq. 19 this case results in $q_{TL}^{*} = q_{\max}$.

### 4.2 LTL shipment size

The second formulation of Model 1 is for LTL service, where the LTL rate estimate of Lecture 3.2 takes the place of the TL charge and the optimal size has no closed form.

Model 1 formulation: Numerical LTL formulation

Using a similar approach, for a given shipment density $s$ and road distance $d$, such that $r_{LTL}(s,q,d)$ can be expressed simply as $r_{LTL}(q)$, the total annual logistics cost for LTL shipments is

$$
\begin{aligned}
TLC_{LTL}(q) &= \frac{f}{q}\max\bigl\{ c_{LTL}(q), MC_{LTL} \bigr\} + \alpha v h q \\
&= f \max\left\{ r_{LTL}(q)\, d, \frac{MC_{LTL}}{q} \right\} + \alpha v h q \\
&\approx \frac{f}{q}\, r_{LTL}(q)\, q d + \alpha v h q = f\, r_{LTL}(q)\, d + \alpha v h q.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
$$

This expression cannot be solved in closed-form to determine the optimal LTL shipment size and, instead, must be solved numerically (using, e.g., Solver in Excel or fminsearch in MATLAB):

$$
q_{LTL}^{*} = \arg\min_{\frac{150}{2000} \le q \le 5} TLC_{LTL}(q)
\tag{22}
$$

where

- $TLC_{LTL}(q)$ = total logistics cost of LTL shipments of size $q$ (\$/yr)
- $r_{LTL}(q)$ = estimated LTL rate for this density and distance (\$/ton-mi)
- $c_{LTL}(q)$ = LTL transport charge (\$)
- $MC_{LTL}$ = LTL minimum charge (\$)
- $q_{LTL}^{*}$ = optimal LTL shipment size (ton).

Example 1(i): Optimal LTL shipment size

Determine the LTL shipment size $q_{LTL}^{*}$ that minimizes the annual TLC for LTL service.

Care is needed in picking bounds for optimization since the LTL formula is only valid for a limited range of values:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_{LTL} &= PPI_{LTL} \left[ \frac{\frac{s^{2}}{8} + 14}{\left( q^{\frac{1}{7}} d^{\frac{15}{29}} - \frac{7}{2} \right)\left( s^{2} + 2 s + 14 \right)} \right] \\
\text{valid for}\quad 37 &\leq d \leq 3354 && \text{(distance, mi)} \\
\frac{150}{2{,}000} &\leq q \leq \frac{10{,}000}{2{,}000} && \text{(weight, ton)} \\
2{,}000\, \frac{q}{s} &\leq 650 && \text{(cube, ft}^{3}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{23}
$$

where

- $PPI_{LTL}$ = producer price index for LTL trucking, as in Lecture 3.2
- $s$ = shipment density (lb/ft3)
- $d$ = road distance (mi).

Together the weight and cube ranges bound the search; the upper bound of 5 tons in Eq. 22 is the case where the cube bound does not bind:

$$
\frac{150}{2000} \leq q \leq \min \left\{ \frac{10{,}000}{2{,}000} , \frac{650 s}{2000} \right\}
\tag{24}
$$

For LTL there is no closed form, and numerical approximation takes over: the TL formula can be done by hand, and the optimal LTL size needs a computer. The LTL rate is a regression, fitted only over a range of values for each parameter. No distance in the data was more than 3,300 miles, so 10,000 miles would be far beyond it; no LTL shipment was more than five tons; and none had more than 650 ft3. A carrier’s website such as FedEx’s or Coyote’s will not even quote an LTL shipment beyond those limits, saying the product cannot be shipped that way, and that is why the optimization must include them.

```julia
# Code block 9: optimal LTL shipment size
ppiLTL = 177.4                     # LTL PPI for Jan 2018

TLC_LTLh(q) = (f/q) * rate_ltl(q, s, d; ppi=ppiLTL) * q * d +
              α*v*h*q

@show LB = 150/2000                # ton (lower bound on q)
@show UB = min(5, 650*s/2000)      # ton (upper bound on q)
@show qᵒLTL = optimize(TLC_LTLh, LB, UB).minimizer   # ton
```

```text
LB = 150 / 2000 = 0.075
UB = min(5, (650s) / 2000) = 1.4444444444444446
qᵒLTL = (optimize(TLC_LTLh, LB, UB)).minimizer = 0.7621710347459996
```

```text
0.7621710347459996
```

$q_{LTL}^{*} =$ 0.7622 ton, inside the valid range from 0.075 to 1.4444 ton.

NoteWithout the bounds

In the random sample of U.S. shipments behind the regression, the shortest distance was about 37 miles and the longest about 3,300, East Coast to West Coast; there is probably nowhere in the world to send LTL 6,000 miles. The lower bound is written as 150 pounds over 2,000 rather than as a small decimal fraction of a ton because 150 pounds is the most that UPS and FedEx will take as a package. A 200-pound shipment has to go by their LTL service, which will also deliver to a residence, so LTL is not only for companies.

The bounds are not a formality, as an unbounded search from a starting point shows. Started at $q_{\max}$, which is above the five-ton limit, the search returns infinity, because the LTL rate is infinite for a shipment larger than 5 tons: the data behind the estimate did not include values in that range, so it would not be valid to extrapolate the formula to them, and the search just spins its wheels. Started instead at the truckload size of 1.9 tons, under 5 tons, it returns infinity again, now because of cube: 1.9 tons of this product is over 850 cubic feet, and an LTL shipment has to be less than 650. A carrier’s website would likewise refuse a quote for a shipment of that size and point to some type of truckload service, which here would likely be a multi-stop shipment, combined by a carrier with other shipments, rather than an independent point-to-point truck; LTL is like UPS or FedEx for a couple of pallets. Started at zero, the search returns zero, below the minimum of 150 pounds, for the same reason: there were no LTL shipments of less than 150 pounds in the data. FedEx’s website would flag such a shipment as invalid or redirect it to its package express service, which takes nothing over 150 pounds; UPS limits a package to 70 pounds, what one person can carry without a hand truck, and other services cover 70 to 150 pounds. LTL starts at 150 pounds and runs to five tons. With the upper bound set by 650 ft3 and the lower by 150 pounds, a starting point between them, such as their geometric mean, is known to be feasible.

Code block 9 needs no starting point, since optimize searches only between the two bounds.

### 4.3 Service choice

Overall, therefore, the optimal independent shipment size is

$$
q_{0}^{*} = \arg\min_{q} \left\{ TLC_{TL}\bigl( q_{TL}^{*} \bigr),\;
TLC_{LTL}\bigl( q_{LTL}^{*} \bigr) \right\}
\tag{25}
$$

where

- $q_{0}^{*}$ = optimal independent shipment size (ton).

Example 1(j): Service choice

Given the optimal TL and LTL shipment sizes, determine which service minimizes annual TLC.

At the optimal LTL size, the total logistics cost of LTL is

$$
TLC_{LTL}\bigl(q_{LTL}^{*}\bigr) = TC_{LTL}\bigl(q_{LTL}^{*}\bigr) + IC\bigl(q_{LTL}^{*}\bigr)
\tag{26}
$$

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# The curves the slides draw, for a product worth v $/ton.
TC_TL(q)  = (f/q)*charge_tl(q, s, d; r = rTL, Kwt = Kwt, Kcu = Kcu,
                            ppi = ppiTL)
TC_LTL(q) = (f/q)*charge_ltl(q, s, d; ppi = ppiLTL)
IC(q, v)  = α*v*h*q
qopt_TL(v)  = sqrt((f*rTL*d)/(α*v*h))
qopt_LTL(v) = optimize(q -> TC_LTL(q) + IC(q, v), LB, UB).minimizer

cred, cblue = RGBf(0.85, 0.10, 0.10), RGBf(0.13, 0.35, 0.60)
cgreen = RGBf(0.10, 0.62, 0.20)

function costcurves!(ax, v)
    qT, qL = qopt_TL(v), qopt_LTL(v)
    rT = range(0.75qL, 1.5qT; length = 400)       # TL curves
    rL = range(0.5qL, 0.99UB; length = 400)
    rI = range(0.5qL, 1.5qT; length = 2)
    TLC_TL(q)  = TC_TL(q) + IC(q, v)
    TLC_LTL(q) = TC_LTL(q) + IC(q, v)
    lines!(ax, rT, TLC_TL; color = cred, linewidth = 2.2)
    lines!(ax, rL, TLC_LTL; color = cred, linewidth = 2.2)
    lines!(ax, rT, TC_TL; color = cblue, linewidth = 2.2)
    lines!(ax, rL, TC_LTL; color = cblue, linewidth = 2.2)
    lines!(ax, rI, q -> IC(q, v); color = cgreen, linewidth = 2.2)
    yT, yL = TLC_TL(qT), TLC_LTL(qL)
    scatter!(ax, [qL, qT], [yL, yT]; color = ink, markersize = 11)
    ax.xticks = ([qL, qT], [@sprintf("%.2f", qL), @sprintf("%.2f", qT)])
    ys = sort([yL, yT])
    ax.yticks = (ys, [commafmt(round(Int, y)) for y in ys])
    # Labels a fixed fraction of the way across the axis.
    x0, x1 = 0.5qL, 1.5qT
    at(p) = x0 + p*(x1 - x0)
    top = max(1.25max(yL, yT), 1.12TLC_LTL(0.99UB))
    lab!(x, y, t, al, o) = text!(ax, x, y; text = t, align = al,
                                 fontsize = 15, color = ink, offset = o)
    # TLC_TL leaves the top of the axis on the left, so its label goes
    # where the curve comes back into view.
    xs = range(at(0.12), x1; length = 400)
    xT = xs[something(findfirst(q -> TLC_TL(q) <= 0.9top, xs), 1)]
    lab!(xT, TLC_TL(xT), L"TLC_{TL}", (:left, :bottom), (6, 2))
    lab!(0.99UB, TLC_LTL(0.99UB), L"TLC_{LTL}", (:right, :bottom), (0, 6))
    lab!(at(0.32), TC_TL(at(0.32)), L"TC_{TL}", (:left, :bottom), (6, 2))
    lab!(at(0.18), TC_LTL(at(0.18)), L"TC_{LTL}", (:right, :top),
         (-2, -6))
    lab!(at(0.35), IC(at(0.35), v), L"IC", (:left, :top), (6, -4))
    xlims!(ax, x0, x1)
    ylims!(ax, IC(x0, v), top)
    return ax
end

fig = Figure(size = (687, 460))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Shipment size (ton)",
          ylabel = "\$ per year", xlabelsize = 16, ylabelsize = 16,
          xticklabelsize = 14, yticklabelsize = 14)
costcurves!(ax, 25_000)
fig
```

Figure 4: Total logistics cost (red), transport cost (blue) and inventory cost (green) for TL and LTL shipments of a product worth \$25,000 per ton, with each service’s optimum marked. The inventory cost is the same for both services; only the transport cost differs.

In Fig. 4 the red lines are the total logistics costs for truckload and for LTL, the blue lines the transport costs, and the green line the inventory cost. There is only one inventory line because the horizontal axis is the size of the load, and once the size is known the inventory cost is the same whichever service carries it; only the transport cost differs, and it differs quite a bit. For this problem, shipping truckload is clearly the better option: 1.9 tons at a time for a minimum total logistics cost of about \$28,500, against about \$40,000 for LTL, which ships a much smaller size but pays much more for it. For LTL the transport and inventory costs are not equal at the optimum; that equality holds only for the truckload square-root formula.

It is better to pick from separate optimal TL and LTL solutions because the independent charge has two local minima:

$$
\begin{aligned}
q^{*}_0 &= \arg\min_q \bigl\{ TLC_\text{TL}(q),\; TLC_\text{LTL}(q) \bigr\} \\
\text{vs.} \quad q^{*}_0 &\overset{!}{=} \arg\min_q \left\{ \frac{f}{q}\, c_0(q) + \alpha v h q \right\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}
$$

Fig. 5 shows the two cases: Fig. 5 (a) is the $v=\$25{,}000$ product (Ex. 1(j), TL selected) and Fig. 5 (b) the $v=\$85{,}000$ product (Ex. 1(k), LTL selected), each plotted as $\ln TLC_0(q)$ over the full range of $q$. Fig. 5 (a) has two clear local optimal solutions that differ from the two optimal solutions for Fig. 5 (b): one shows the case where truckload is better (Fig. 5 (a)), the other where LTL is better (Fig. 5 (b)). Because the independent charge $c_0(q)$ has a kink at the TL/LTL crossover, traditional univariate nonlinear optimization techniques could get stuck in the second-best local optimal solution. By taking the best of TL and LTL, first the TL is computed directly (analytically), and then the LTL has a single local optimal solution, the resulting procedure is much more robust and better able to find the global optimum, which is what minTLC does, in the pseudocode below.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# c0, the independent charge of Sec. 2.3's figure, takes the cheaper
# service at every size, so minimizing TLC with it directly faces both
# services' minima at once.
lnTLC0(q, v) = log((f/q)*c0(q) + IC(q, v))

function lnpanel(vi, qhi)
    fig = Figure(size = (340, 380))
    axv = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Shipment size (ton)",
               ylabel = L"\ln TLC_0(q)", xlabelsize = 15,
               ylabelsize = 15, xticklabelsize = 13, yticklabelsize = 13)
    qs = range(LB, qhi; length = 1500)
    lines!(axv, qs, q -> lnTLC0(q, vi); color = cblue, linewidth = 2)
    qT, qL = qopt_TL(vi), qopt_LTL(vi)
    scatter!(axv, [qL, qT], [lnTLC0(qL, vi), lnTLC0(qT, vi)];
             color = ink, markersize = 10)
    xlims!(axv, LB, qhi)
    return fig
end
lnpanel(25_000, qmax)
lnpanel(85_000, 1.8qopt_TL(85_000))
```

(a) \$25,000 per ton: TL selected

(b) \$85,000 per ton: LTL selected

Figure 5: The logarithm of total logistics cost when the independent charge chooses TL or LTL for each size. Each curve has two local minima, one for each service, separated by the kink where the charge changes from LTL to TL.

One way to solve the problem with both services would be to combine them, letting the transport cost at each size be whichever of LTL and truckload is cheaper, and then find the quantity that minimizes that combined equation. Plotted over a range of sizes, as in Fig. 5, the combined total logistics cost has the point to pick, but an optimization finds only local minima, so it would have to start in the right basin to reach it; with different numbers the lower cost would be in the other region, so deciding where to look is itself a difficult problem. The way to avoid it is to calculate the truckload optimum first, then the LTL optimum, and take the smaller of the two. Combining them may seem the obvious way; this way is less immediately obvious, but much more robust, and it avoids the problem of two local minima altogether.

Model 1 formulation: Separate TL and LTL procedure

```text
algorithm minTLC;
{ input:  shipment f, s, α, v, h, d; carrier r, K_wt, K_cu, PPI_TL;
          and PPI_LTL                                               }
{ output: size q*, cost TLC*, and whether LTL is chosen             }
begin
    q_TL := min{ √( f · max{r·d, MC_TL} / (α·v·h) ), q_max };
    q* := q_TL, TLC* := TLC_TL(q_TL), isLTL := false;
    q_LTL := arg min{ TLC_LTL(q) : 150/2000 ≤ q ≤ min{5, 650·s/2000} };
    if TLC_LTL(q_LTL) < TLC* then
        q* := q_LTL, TLC* := TLC_LTL(q_LTL), isLTL := true;
    return (q*, TLC*, isLTL);
end;
```

Example 1(k): Service choice at higher product value

If the unit value of the product rises to $v = \$85{,}000$/ton, re-determine the optimal shipment sizes and which service is selected.

For a given lane and a given product (density and weight) at a given annual demand, the value of the load, $v$, becomes the critical factor in determining whether LTL or TL is the preferred mode since cycle inventory costs increase as the load value increases, but transportation costs remain unchanged.
