```text
qᵒTL = sqrt((f * rTL * d) / (α * v * h)) = 1.0317302108505633
TCᵒ_TL = (f / qᵒTL) * rTL * d = 26309.12037668936
ICᵒ_TL = α * v * h * qᵒTL = 26309.120376689363
TLCᵒ_TL = TCᵒ_TL + ICᵒ_TL = 52618.24075337872
qᵒLTL = (optimize(TLC_LTLh, LB, UB)).minimizer = 0.2735447301881209
rLTL = 3.836994200243633
cLTL = rLTL * qᵒLTL * d = 558.3816370031636
TCᵒ_LTL = (f / qᵒLTL) * cLTL = 40825.618290592254
ICᵒ_LTL = α * v * h * qᵒLTL = 6975.390619797084
TLCᵒ_LTL = TCᵒ_LTL + ICᵒ_LTL = 47801.00891038934
LTL selected
```

$q_{TL}^{*} =$ 1.0317 ton at \$52,618.24/yr against $q_{LTL}^{*} =$ 0.2735 ton at \$47,801.01/yr, so LTL is selected at \$85,000 per ton.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
fig = Figure(size = (687, 420))
for (i, vi) in enumerate((25_000, 85_000))
    axv = Axis(fig[1, i]; xlabel = "Shipment size (ton)",
               ylabel = i == 1 ? "\$ per year" : "",
               title = "($('a' + i - 1)) \$$(commafmt(vi)) per ton",
               titlesize = 16, xlabelsize = 15, ylabelsize = 15,
               xticklabelsize = 13, yticklabelsize = 13)
    costcurves!(axv, vi)
end
fig
```

Figure 6: The costs of Fig. 4 for a product worth (a) \$25,000 and (b) \$85,000 per ton. At the higher value the inventory cost line is steeper, both optimal sizes are smaller, and LTL has the lower total logistics cost.

With everything else the same and only the value raised from \$25,000 to \$85,000 per ton, things flip: truckload now costs about \$5,000 a year more than LTL. The higher value has raised the inventory cost, inventory is more significant, and LTL is the better choice. That is the direction to expect: if the value were to triple, LTL should become more likely, not less. This is the Nudge check of Lecture 1.2: raise one input and confirm that the answer moves the way it should. Getting the general trends right always matters when working with a computer, because it is easy to put numbers in and get extreme results. A mental model of the overall trends to expect is what flags a result that has gone wrong, before giving a manager a result that goes exactly the wrong direction. As the value of the product goes higher and higher, the shipment size gets smaller, and eventually so small that it is better to ship LTL, even though the transport is more expensive, because LTL can ship smaller quantities. The value works like a slider from \$25,000 to \$85,000 per ton, along which the decision switches from truckload to LTL, and the switch is strictly a function of the value going up.

To make it easier to work with shipment data, a named tuple tr can be used to store rate and capacity limits for TL shipments, and shipment-related information can be stored in a DataFrame sh. These can then be used as inputs into a series of functions.

Model 1 implementation: Minimum-TLC shipment size

```julia
# Model: minimum-TLC shipment size
# sh: Per-shipment parameters; a NamedTuple or DataFrameRow with fields f
#    (demand, ton/yr), s (density, lb/ft³), a (inventory fraction), v
#    (unit value, $/ton), h (holding rate, 1/yr), d (distance, mi).
# tr: Carrier NamedTuple with fields r, Kwt, Kcu, ppi (TL). Pass nothing
#    for LTL-only mode.
# ppi: LTL Producer Price Index scalar. Pass nothing for TL-only mode.
minTLC     # (sh) -> qᵒ
```

```julia
# Code block 12: Ex. 1(k) again, with the function
tr = (r = rTL, Kwt = Kwt, Kcu = Kcu, ppi = ppiTL)
sh = DataFrame(f = f, s = s, a = α, v = v, h = h, d = d)
res = minTLC(first(sh), tr, ppiLTL)
@show res.qᵒ                       # ton
@show res.TLCᵒ                     # $/yr
@show res.isLTL                    # LTL selected?
```

```text
res.qᵒ = 0.27354473025205917
res.TLCᵒ = 47801.00891038934
res.isLTL = true
```

```text
true
```

minTLC(sh, tr [, ppi]) returns a NamedTuple (qᵒ, TLCᵒ, isLTL), the cost-minimizing shipment size, the resulting TLC, and a Boolean indicating whether LTL was chosen, for a single shipment row, letting the next two parts stay short.

## 5. Aggregate periodic shipment

Up until this point, only one product has been handled. The most important idea when shipping multiple products together is that all of the products can be treated as a single aggregate product: every formula for the optimal shipment size of a single product carries over to the aggregate product, with each model parameter replaced by its aggregate counterpart. This aggregate shipment typically never occurs in practice because there might be thousands of different potential items; instead, different small subsets of these items would comprise each actual load that is transported over the course of a year.

### 5.1 Second product

A second product is now shipped point-to-point from the same origin to the same destination, and its shipment is determined on its own before the two are combined in Sec. 5.2.

Example 1(l): A second product

On Jan 10, 2018, determine the optimal independent shipment size and TLC for a second product, 80 ton/yr of Class 60 material worth \$5,000/ton, shipped point-to-point from Raleigh to Gainesville, as before.

The size of the second product is not given, only that it is a Class 60 product, and what is needed is its density. The class-density table, Table 8 in Lecture 3.2, gives the average density for each class, so for Class 60 the density is 32.16 lb/ft3. Everything else is the same as for the first product.

```julia
# Code block 13: a second product
push!(sh, first(sh))                     # duplicate the row
sh[2, [:f, :s, :v]] = [80, 32.16, 5000]  # patch the second product
sh.qmax = [maxpayld(row, tr) for row in eachrow(sh)]
transform!(sh, AsTable(:) =>
    ByRow(row -> minTLC(row, tr, ppiLTL)) => AsTable)
prt(sh)
```

```text
    f      s  a       v       h    d   qmax    qᵒ       TLCᵒ  isLTL
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1  20   4.44  1  85,000  0.3000  532   6.11  0.27  47,801.01      1
2  80  32.16  1   5,000  0.3000  532  25.00  8.51  25,523.60      0
```

Second product: $q_0^{*} =$ 8.5079 ton by TL, $TLC^{*} =$ \$25,523.60/yr; its maximum payload, 25.0 ton, is set by weight.

What differs from the first product is that its weight and cube per carton were given, so its density could be worked out, and density matters twice: it is a parameter in the maximum payload, $q_{\max}$, and in the LTL rate. For the second product only the class is given, so its density comes from the table.

### 5.2 Aggregate shipment

Since for periodic shipments $q$ is not given and must be determined, $f$ can be used in place of $q$ when determining the aggregate demand and density of multiple items shipped together as part of a single load (cf. the aggregate shipment formulas, Eq. 10 in Lecture 3.2):

$$
f_{agg} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} f_i , \qquad
s_{agg} = \frac{f_{agg}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{f_i}{s_i}} .
\tag{28}
$$

Also, the aggregate value is the demand-weighted sum of the values of the items:

$$
v_{agg} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{f_i}{f_{agg}}\, v_i
\tag{29}
$$

where

- $f_i$ = annual demand of item $i$ (ton/yr)
- $s_i$ = density of item $i$ (lb/ft3)
- $v_i$ = unit value of item $i$ (\$/ton)
- $m$ = number of items shipped together
- $f_{agg}$ = annual demand of the aggregate (ton/yr)
- $s_{agg}$ = density of the aggregate (lb/ft3)
- $v_{agg}$ = unit value of the aggregate (\$/ton).

The second product is not introduced just to repeat the calculation. With two products going from the same facility to the same customer, there would never be two separate trucks, one for each, which is what the separate calculations assume, whether TL or LTL; the products would be put on the same truck, and that means treating them as one aggregate product. With the same origin and destination the distance is the same, and here $\alpha$ and $h$ are the same too; what differs is the quantity, 20 plus 80 for 100 tons in aggregate. The value is a demand-weighted average, each product’s value weighted by its share of total demand, which gives \$21,000 per ton between the \$85,000 and the \$5,000, and $h$ and $\alpha$ could be averaged the same way. Density is a different animal. Taking density as a weighted average does not work out right; the math says it is the aggregate weight over the aggregate cube, which puts the aggregate demand in the numerator and the sum of each product’s demand over its density in the denominator, giving 14.31 lb/ft3. Density is the one aggregate that is not obvious.

Example 1(m): Aggregate shipment

Determine the annual TLC if the two products are always shipped together on the same truck, and compare to the sum of their independent TLCs.

For this example, with $d_1 = d_2$, $h_1 = h_2$, and $\alpha_1 = \alpha_2$, the optimal TL size of the aggregate is

$$
q_{TL}^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{f_{agg}\, r d}{\alpha\, v_{agg}\, h}}
\tag{30}
$$

```julia
# Code block 14: the aggregate shipment
@show fagg = sum(sh.f)                   # ton/yr
@show sagg = fagg/sum(sh.f ./ sh.s)      # lb/ft^3
@show vagg = sum(sh.f .* sh.v)/fagg      # $/ton

ash = aggshmt(sh[:, [:f, :s, :a, :v, :h, :d]])   # the same, by Logjam
@show qmax_agg = maxpayld(ash, tr)       # ton
resa = minTLC(ash, tr)                   # TL only
@show TLC_indep = sum(sh.TLCᵒ)           # $/yr, shipped separately
@show TLC_agg = resa.TLCᵒ                # $/yr, shipped together
```

```text
fagg = sum(sh.f) = 100
sagg = fagg / sum(sh.f ./ sh.s) = 14.311142755428978
vagg = sum(sh.f .* sh.v) / fagg = 21000.0
qmax_agg = maxpayld(ash, tr) = 19.677821288714846
TLC_indep = sum(sh.TLCᵒ) = 73324.60472925525
TLC_agg = resa.TLCᵒ = 58481.90492370572
```

```text
58481.90492370572
```

Shipped separately, the two products cost \$73,324.60/yr; shipped together as one aggregate in loads of 4.6414 ton, they cost \$58,481.90/yr, a saving of \$14,842.70/yr.

Show the code that builds the table

```julia
# Code block 15: the two products and their aggregate, as a table
tdays(q, f) = 365.25q/f            # interval between shipments, days
fmt(x, dg) = x === missing ? "" : @sprintf("%.*f", dg, x)
cm(x) = x === missing ? "" : commafmt(round(Int, x))
rows = [("1", sh.f[1], sh.s[1], sh.v[1], sh.qmax[1], sh.TLCᵒ[1],
         sh.qᵒ[1]),
        ("2", sh.f[2], sh.s[2], sh.v[2], sh.qmax[2], sh.TLCᵒ[2],
         sh.qᵒ[2]),
        ("1 + 2", missing, missing, missing, missing, TLC_indep, missing),
        ("Aggregate", ash.f, ash.s, ash.v, qmax_agg, TLC_agg, resa.qᵒ)]
println("| | \$f\$ | \$s\$ | \$v\$ | \$q_{\\max}\$ | \$TLC\$ | ",
        "\$q^{*}\$ | \$t\$ |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for (lab, f_, s_, v_, qm, tlc, q_) in rows
    t_ = (q_ === missing) ? missing : tdays(q_, f_)
    println("| ", lab, " | ", cm(f_), " | ", fmt(s_, 2), " | ", cm(v_),
            " | ", fmt(qm, 2), " | ", tlc === missing ? "" : usd(tlc),
            " | ", fmt(q_, 2), " | ", fmt(t_, 2), " |")
end
println("\n: The two products shipped separately and as one aggregate: ",
        "\$f\$ in ton/yr, \$s\$ in lb/ft^3^, \$v\$ in \\\$/ton, ",
        "\$q_{\\max}\$ and \$q^{*}\$ in ton, \$TLC\$ in \\\$/yr, and ",
        "the interval \$t\$ in days. ",
        "{#tbl-shipment-economics .dense .fit}\n")
```

Table 3: The two products shipped separately and as one aggregate: $f$ in ton/yr, $s$ in lb/ft3, $v$ in \$/ton, $q_{\max}$ and $q^{*}$ in ton, $TLC$ in \$/yr, and the interval $t$ in days.

| | $f$ | $s$ | $v$ | $q_{\max}$ | $TLC$ | $q^{*}$ | $t$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 | 4.44 | 85,000 | 6.11 | 47,801.01 | 0.27 | 5.00 |
| 2 | 80 | 32.16 | 5,000 | 25.00 | 25,523.60 | 8.51 | 38.84 |
| 1 + 2 | | | | | 73,324.60 | | |
| Aggregate | 100 | 14.31 | 21,000 | 19.68 | 58,481.90 | 4.64 | 16.95 |

Table 3 sets the two products against their aggregate. Shipped separately at their own optima, the two products cost about \$73,000 a year in total logistics cost, and as an aggregate about \$58,000, so aggregate shipments save money. What makes the technique particularly useful is that it is not limited to two products. For a company with thousands of different SKUs, a single aggregate product can represent all of them: any one truck carries maybe several dozen or a hundred of the thousand, a kind of random draw, but the aggregate of the thousand can be used for many location problems. The aggregate shipment assumption works especially well with hundreds or thousands of products, and it makes location trade-offs and much other analysis possible, which is what makes it so powerful.

The assumption is not that every shipment to every customer carries all 1,000 products. On average perhaps 20 or 25 different products go on a truck, like drawing a sample of 25 chips out of a bucket of 1,000 for each customer, and on average all of the chips can be treated as a single aggregate shipment. Any one shipment will have a density, and a value, a little higher or a little lower than the aggregate, so the aggregate is not accurate for one shipment. But over more than 10 or 15 customers, and even with as few as a few dozen products, the law of large numbers takes over: sometimes a little too much, sometimes a little too little, and done enough times the result approaches the aggregate almost exactly. So instead of a detailed analysis, a company with 1,000 products shipping to 100 customers can quickly get an estimate of its cost, probably to within plus or minus 5%, which is enough to start making decisions. It works surprisingly well. More detailed analysis, when tried, turned out to give results that were probably worse, because a more complicated model brings in assumptions that are not right and more room for error. Simple is better.

Table 3 also shows a Bounds check, from Lecture 1.2, on an aggregation: the aggregate’s value should fall within the range of the values being aggregated, as \$21,000 falls between \$85,000 and \$5,000, and if it were greater or less than both, something would be wrong in the aggregation. The same holds for density, which should be somewhere in the middle of the densities it is composed from; the annual demands are simply added.

Example 2: Interval-constrained full truckload

On average, 200 tons of components are shipped 750 miles from a fabrication plant to an assembly plant each year. The components are produced and consumed at a constant rate throughout the year. Currently, full truckloads of the material are shipped. Determine the impact on total annual logistics costs if TL shipments were made every two weeks. The revenue per loaded truck-mile is \$2.00; a truck’s cubic and weight capacities are 3,000 ft3 and 24 tons, respectively; each ton of the material is valued at \$5,000 and has a density of 10 lb per ft3; the material loses 30% of its value after 18 months; and in-transit inventory costs can be ignored.

The truck capacities here are not the standard ones. The loss of 30% of the material’s value after 18 months is its obsolescence, and it gives the obsolescence component of cost. With a problem statement like this, it is good practice to decide how it will be modeled and to relate the problem to the model’s variables. The obsolescence factor follows directly from Eq. 13: the 0.3 reduction in value over 18 months, or one and a half years, gives 0.2, and combining it with the default interest and warehousing components gives 0.31 as the overall carrying rate. Production is constant here; with batch production, which is probably more common, $\alpha$ would be zero plus one half, or one half. The full-truckload size is the maximum payload. LTL is not considered, since the problem concerns only truckloads, although in general it is a good idea at least to consider it: shipping more frequently makes the loads smaller, and LTL may then be the better option.

```julia
# Code block 16: TLC of full truckloads
d2 = 750                           # mi
s2 = 10                            # lb/ft^3
Kwt2, Kcu2 = 24, 3000              # ton, ft^3
r2 = 2                             # $/mi
f2 = 200                           # ton/yr
v2 = 5000                          # $/ton
@show hobs2 = 0.3/1.5              # 1/yr: 30% of value lost in 1.5 yr
@show h2 = 0.11 + hobs2            # 1/yr: interest + warehousing 0.11
a2 = 1                             # constant production and consumption
@show qmax2 = maxpayld(s2; Kwt = Kwt2, Kcu = Kcu2)      # ton
@show cFTL2 = charge_tl(qmax2, s2, d2; r = r2,
                        Kwt = Kwt2, Kcu = Kcu2)         # $
@show TLC_FTL2 = totlogcost(qmax2, cFTL2, f2, a2, v2, h2)  # $/yr
```

```text
hobs2 = 0.3 / 1.5 = 0.19999999999999998
h2 = 0.11 + hobs2 = 0.31
qmax2 = maxpayld(s2; Kwt = Kwt2, Kcu = Kcu2) = 15.0
cFTL2 = charge_tl(qmax2, s2, d2; r = r2, Kwt = Kwt2, Kcu = Kcu2) = 1500.0
TLC_FTL2 = totlogcost(qmax2, cFTL2, f2, a2, v2, h2) = 43250.0
```

```text
43250.0
```

```julia
# Code block 17: TLC of two-week shipments
@show nFTL2 = f2/qmax2             # TL/yr
@show tmax2 = 2*7/365.25           # yr/TL
@show nmin2 = 1/tmax2              # TL/yr
@show q2wk = f2/max(nFTL2, nmin2)  # ton
@show c2wk = charge_tl(q2wk, s2, d2; r = r2,
                       Kwt = Kwt2, Kcu = Kcu2)          # $
@show TLC_2wk = totlogcost(q2wk, c2wk, f2, a2, v2, h2)   # $/yr
@show ΔTLC = TLC_2wk - TLC_FTL2    # $/yr
```

```text
nFTL2 = f2 / qmax2 = 13.333333333333334
tmax2 = (2 * 7) / 365.25 = 0.038329911019849415
nmin2 = 1 / tmax2 = 26.089285714285715
q2wk = f2 / max(nFTL2, nmin2) = 7.665982203969883
c2wk = charge_tl(q2wk, s2, d2; r = r2, Kwt = Kwt2, Kcu = Kcu2) = 1500.0
TLC_2wk = totlogcost(q2wk, c2wk, f2, a2, v2, h2) = 51016.20098758189
ΔTLC = TLC_2wk - TLC_FTL2 = 7766.200987581891
```

```text
7766.200987581891
```

$TLC_{FTL} =$ \$43,250.00/yr and $TLC_{2wk} =$ \$51,016.20/yr, so shipping every two weeks increases total logistics cost by \$7,766.20 per year. At 7.67 ton the two-week shipments are still truckloads, so LTL is not considered.

As a logistics engineer, that is where the analysis stops: the manager takes it further and decides whether about \$7,000 a year is important and worth the change, but at least there is a dollar figure for the impact. A two-week interval would typically come from the destination: a manager at the assembly plant who does not want monthly shipments because there is nowhere to store the product. Or the 200 tons a year, assumed constant, may in reality change quite a bit, so that with whole truckloads an increase in demand could force a smaller extra truckload to be shipped just because of running out of stock; the real world is not constant. The 5% and 6% for interest and warehousing are default values to use when a problem gives none, just as 2,750 ft3 and 25 tons are the truck capacities unless others are called out. The assumption of constant demand and production is the most bothersome one, since very few products have that kind of consistency. But even under it, the problem can simply be recalculated every two weeks, so assuming constancy is not locking in a year, and in practice it is not much of an issue.

The cost might still be worth incurring if the customer wants to be able to change its order size every two weeks rather than receive a month’s worth of inventory at a time, because things change so much that it does not want to be stuck with obsolete inventory. If the customer is willing to do this despite a calculated increase of about \$7,000, that only means the model does not incorporate all of the factors: some of the customer’s considerations are not in it.
